    Going Deeper: Proofs, Cipher Design and Crypto in Hidden Places

    🤔 You know which tools to use. Now meet the games that define “secure”, the tricks that break ciphers, and the hidden crypto inside Tor, “Sign in with Google”, your bank card and your laptop’s boot screen.

    • ⏱️ ~22 min
    • 📚 10 sections
    • 🎮 8 interactive
    • ⭐ 320 XP
    • 🔑 1 fragment

    The first nineteen chapters explained what each tool does and which one to pick. This chapter lifts the lid on three things most guides skip: how cryptographers define and prove "secure," how ciphers are built and broken, and the cryptography hiding inside Tor, "Sign in with Google," your bank card and your laptop's startup screen. It ends with the long political fight over who gets to use strong encryption.

    You still don't need any math. Every idea comes with a picture, an analogy or a game.

    20.1What "secure" means: security games#

    "This cipher is secure" sounds like an opinion. Cryptographers turn it into something you can test, by describing a game between a challenger (who holds the key) and an attacker. A scheme is secure if no realistic attacker can win the game noticeably more often than by guessing.

    The classic game: IND-CPA ("indistinguishability under chosen-plaintext attack").

    This one game captures a lot:

    • It forbids patterns. If the ciphertext leaked even one bit about the message (its first letter, whether it contains "YES"), the attacker would pick two messages that differ in that bit and win.
    • It forbids deterministic encryption. If the same message always gives the same ciphertext, the attacker simply asks the challenger to encrypt M0 in step 1 and compares. That is exactly why ECB mode (Chapter 5) and textbook RSA (Chapter 9) fail, and why real encryption needs a random IV or a unique nonce.
    • Length is allowed to leak. The two messages must be the same length, because almost all encryption reveals length. (The CRIME and BREACH attacks in Chapter 18 exploited exactly that.)

    The idea behind this game is called semantic security: the ciphertext tells you nothing useful about the plaintext except its length. Shafi Goldwasser and Silvio Micali formalized it in 1982 and later won the Turing Award, computing's highest honor, partly for it.

    Stronger and other games:

    Security notion What the attacker may do What it rules out Schemes that meet it
    IND-CPA Get any messages encrypted Patterns, deterministic encryption AES-CTR or AES-CBC with random IVs
    IND-CCA (chosen-ciphertext) Also get any ciphertext decrypted, except the challenge Malleability: tweaking a ciphertext and learning from the result AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305, RSA-OAEP, HPKE
    INT-CTXT (ciphertext integrity) Try to create any new ciphertext that decrypts successfully Forgery Every AEAD
    EUF-CMA (unforgeability) Get signatures or MAC tags on any messages Forging a valid tag or signature on a new message HMAC, Ed25519, ECDSA, RSA-PSS

    IND-CCA matters because real systems do decrypt whatever arrives and react to it. Bleichenbacher's 1998 attack on RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 (Chapter 9) and padding-oracle attacks (Chapter 18) are both chosen-ciphertext attacks: the attacker sends modified ciphertexts and watches the error messages. AEAD (authenticated encryption) gives you IND-CCA plus INT-CTXT in one package.

    🧪 Try it yourself (Python): play the IND-CPA game against ECB, then see why randomized encryption survives it.

    Python
    import secrets
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.ciphers import Cipher, algorithms, modes
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.ciphers.aead import AESGCM

key = secrets.token_bytes(16)
def ecb(m):                                         # deterministic: same input, same output
    enc = Cipher(algorithms.AES(key), modes.ECB()).encryptor()
    return enc.update(m) + enc.finalize()

m0, m1 = b"ATTACK AT DAWN!!", b"RETREAT AT TEN!!"   # equal length: 16 bytes each
b = secrets.randbelow(2)                            # the challenger's secret coin
challenge = ecb([m0, m1][b])

# The attacker may ask for encryptions of anything (chosen plaintexts)...
guess = 0 if ecb(m0) == challenge else 1
print("attacker wins:", guess == b)                 # always True

aes = AESGCM(AESGCM.generate_key(bit_length=128))
c1 = aes.encrypt(secrets.token_bytes(12), m0, None)
c2 = aes.encrypt(secrets.token_bytes(12), m0, None)
print(c1 == c2)                                     # False: same message, different ciphertexts

    💡 Key idea: "Secure" always means "secure against a specific attacker who can do specific things." When you read that a scheme is IND-CCA secure, it means: even an attacker who can get anything else decrypted learns nothing from the ciphertext you care about.

    20.2Security proofs, reductions and the random oracle model#

    Once "secure" is a game, you can try to prove that a scheme wins it. Cryptographic proofs almost never say "this is unbreakable." They say something more modest and more useful:

    If someone could break this scheme, then they could also solve a problem everyone believes is hard.

    This is called a reduction. Analogy: you can't prove that nobody will ever pick your new lock. But you can prove "anyone who picks my lock can also open a bank vault of a famous design that has resisted every thief for 50 years." That's strong evidence your lock is good.

    Examples of what reductions connect:

    Scheme "Breaking it would mean…"
    Diffie-Hellman key exchange Solving a Diffie-Hellman-style discrete-log problem (Chapter 10)
    RSA-OAEP Inverting RSA without the private key (Chapter 9)
    HMAC Breaking the hash function's internal compression step
    ML-KEM (Kyber) Solving a hard lattice problem (Chapter 17)
    Encrypt-then-MAC Breaking either the cipher or the MAC (Chapter 7)

    Models: the fine print. Some proofs only work in a simplified world. The most famous is the random oracle model (Bellare and Rogaway, 1993): the proof pretends the hash function is a perfect magic box that returns a fresh random answer for every new input. Real hash functions such as SHA-256 aren't magic boxes, but they behave very much like them, and proofs in this model (RSA-OAEP, Ed25519 and Schnorr signatures, many post-quantum KEMs) have held up well in practice. A proof that doesn't need this idealization is said to be in the standard model, and is considered stronger.

    What a proof does not cover:

    • The model's assumptions. If the "hard problem" turns out to be easy (as quantum computers would make factoring), the proof says nothing.
    • Implementation. A proof is about the algorithm on paper. Timing leaks, bad random numbers and buffer overflows (Chapter 18) live outside it.
    • Mistakes in the proof itself. Proofs are written by humans.

    📜 True story: a gap in a famous proof. RSA-OAEP was published with a security proof in 1994. In 2001, Victor Shoup showed that the proof had a gap: it didn't actually prove what everyone thought. The scheme turned out to be fine (other researchers quickly repaired the proof the same year), but it was a reminder that "provably secure" deserves the same scrutiny as any other claim.

    And here's a surprise: AES has no security proof at all. There is no reduction to a famous hard problem. Its security comes from 25 years of the world's best cryptanalysts attacking it and failing (next two sections). For symmetric ciphers and hash functions, that public battle-testing is the evidence.

    💡 Key idea: A security proof turns "trust me" into "trust this well-studied hard problem, in this model, assuming the code matches the paper." It's powerful, but it is one ingredient of confidence, not a guarantee.

    ⚖️ Pros & Cons

    Kinds of evidence that a scheme is secure

    💡 Concept
    Proof in the standard model

    Reduction with no idealized parts

    • Strongest kind of proof
    • No “pretend the hash is magic” step
    • Schemes are often slower or bigger
    • Still only as good as the hard problem and the code
    Best for: High-assurance designs
    💡 Concept
    Proof in the random oracle model

    Treats the hash as a perfect random function

    • Allows fast, practical schemes (RSA-OAEP, Ed25519, ML-KEM)
    • Excellent real-world track record
    • Real hashes aren’t random oracles
    • Contrived schemes exist that are “proven” yet breakable
    Best for: Most modern public-key schemes
    💡 Concept
    Survived public cryptanalysis

    No proof, decades of attacks (AES, SHA-2)

    • Tested against every known attack technique
    • Allows very fast designs
    • A brand-new technique could appear
    • Needs ongoing, open scrutiny
    Best for: Block ciphers and hash functions
    ❌ Avoid
    “Provably unbreakable” marketing

    Claims without a published model

    • None
    • No stated game, assumptions or review means no proof
    • Often a sign of home-made crypto
    Best for: Treat as a red flag

    20.3How block ciphers are built: Feistel networks, SPNs and ARX#

    Chapter 5 showed AES as a Rubik's cube of rounds. Designers use a few standard blueprints for those rounds.

    1. The Feistel network (invented by Horst Feistel at IBM in the early 1970s; used by DES).

    Split the block into a left half and a right half. Each round, scramble the right half with a round key, XOR the result into the left half, then swap:

    The magic: F doesn't have to be reversible. It can be any scrambling function, even a one-way hash. To decrypt, you run the very same rounds with the keys in reverse order, because XOR-ing the same F output twice cancels out (Chapter 3). That made Feistel designs easy to build in 1970s hardware: one circuit both encrypts and decrypts.

    🧪 Try it yourself (Python): a toy 2-byte Feistel cipher whose round function is a SHA-256 hash, which can't be reversed. Decryption still works.

    Python
    import hashlib

def F(half: int, key: bytes) -> int:
    # Any scrambling function works, even a one-way hash!
    return hashlib.sha256(key + bytes([half])).digest()[0]

def feistel(block: bytes, keys, decrypt=False):
    L, R = block[0], block[1]
    for k in (reversed(keys) if decrypt else keys):
        L, R = R, L ^ F(R, k)
    return bytes([R, L])                     # swap the halves at the end

keys = [b"k1", b"k2", b"k3", b"k4"]
ct = feistel(b"Hi", keys)
print(ct.hex())                              # ebda
print(feistel(ct, keys, decrypt=True))       # b'Hi'

    (Never use this for real data: a 16-bit block and four rounds are toys.)

    2. The substitution–permutation network (SPN) (used by AES). Instead of halves, every round transforms the whole block: substitute bytes through an S-box (confusion), then shuffle and mix them (diffusion), then add the round key. Every step must be reversible, so decryption runs inverse steps. SPNs spread changes faster, which is one reason AES needs only 10 to 14 rounds where DES needed 16.

    3. ARX (Add–Rotate–XOR): use only those three cheap CPU operations, repeated many times. ChaCha20 (Chapter 5) and BLAKE2/BLAKE3 (Chapter 6) are built this way. ARX is fast on any processor and naturally constant-time, because none of its operations depend on secret-indexed lookup tables.

    Design Ciphers Strengths Weaknesses
    Feistel DES, 3DES, Blowfish, Twofish, Camellia Round function needn't be reversible; same circuit decrypts Only half the block changes per round, so it needs more rounds
    SPN AES, Serpent, PRESENT Fast diffusion; well-understood design theory Needs reversible S-boxes; table lookups can leak timing in software
    ARX ChaCha20, Salsa20, BLAKE2/3, Speck Fast everywhere; constant-time by nature Harder to analyze; needs many rounds

    Why so many rounds? One round of any of these is weak. Each round adds a layer of confusion and diffusion, and attacks typically work against reduced versions first. Designers choose a round count well above the best attack: that buffer is called the security margin.

    ✏️ sketching an interactive demo…

    Cipher blueprints

    👍 Situational
    Feistel network

    Split in halves, mix one into the other

    • Round function needn’t be reversible
    • Same circuit encrypts and decrypts
    • Half the block changes per round, so more rounds
    • Its famous member (DES) is retired
    Best for: DES, 3DES, Blowfish, Twofish, Camellia
    ✅ Use it
    SPN

    Substitute, permute, add key: whole block per round

    • Fast diffusion, fewer rounds
    • Rich design theory (AES)
    • Needs reversible S-boxes
    • Table lookups can leak timing in software
    Best for: AES, Serpent, PRESENT
    ✅ Use it
    ARX

    Only Add, Rotate, XOR

    • Fast on any CPU
    • Constant-time by nature
    • Harder to analyze
    • Needs many rounds
    Best for: ChaCha20, BLAKE2/3

    20.4How ciphers get broken: the cryptanalyst's toolbox#

    Brute force tries every key. Cryptanalysis looks for shortcuts: statistical patterns that survive all the rounds. Here are the big ideas, without the math.

    Differential cryptanalysis: follow the difference. Encrypt pairs of plaintexts that differ in a chosen way, and watch how that difference travels through the cipher. For a perfect cipher, the output differences would look completely random. For a real one, some input differences lead to some output differences more often than they should. An S-box is the key ingredient: here's what happens inside the 4-bit S-box of the lightweight cipher PRESENT:

    4/16 sounds bad, but it is actually the best any 4-bit S-box can achieve: perfection is impossible, so designers aim for "as flat as possible." Attackers chain these "lucky" paths across rounds. If the chain holds more often than chance predicts, it reveals bits of the last round's key. The defense: S-boxes whose best path is as unlikely as possible, and enough rounds that every chain becomes hopelessly improbable.

    📜 True story: IBM knew in 1974. Eli Biham and Adi Shamir published differential cryptanalysis around 1990 and found that DES resisted it surprisingly well. In 1994, IBM's Don Coppersmith revealed why: IBM had discovered the technique while designing DES in 1974, tuned the S-boxes against it, and agreed with the NSA to keep it secret. The mysterious S-boxes that had fueled backdoor rumors for 20 years were actually protecting DES.

    Linear cryptanalysis: find a lopsided coin. Look for a simple relationship between some plaintext bits, some ciphertext bits and some key bits that holds a little more (or less) than 50% of the time. With enough known plaintext–ciphertext pairs, the bias reveals key bits. Mitsuru Matsui published it in 1993 and, in 1994, recovered a real DES key using 2⁴³ known plaintexts: the first experimental attack on full DES faster than brute force.

    Other tools in the box:

    Attack Idea Famous result
    Meet-in-the-middle Encrypt from the front and decrypt from the back, and match in the middle Why "double DES" is barely stronger than DES, and 3DES was used instead (Chapter 5)
    Related-key Study encryptions under keys that differ in known ways A 2009 attack on AES-256 needs 2⁹⁹·⁵ steps, but only if the attacker can make you use related keys
    Slide attack Exploit rounds that are all identical Breaks ciphers with weak key schedules, whatever the number of rounds
    Algebraic Write the cipher as huge systems of equations and solve them Mostly theoretical against modern ciphers
    Biclique Advanced brute-force bookkeeping Best known attack on full AES-128: about 2¹²⁶ work, barely better than 2¹²⁸

    What "broken" means to a cryptographer. Academic papers call a cipher "broken" when any attack beats brute force, even if it needs more energy than the Sun will ever produce. AES-128 has been "broken" by 2 bits since 2011, and it is still perfectly safe. In practice, worry when an attack becomes feasible (DES in 1998, SHA-1 in 2017), not when it becomes publishable.

    💡 Key idea: Ciphers earn trust by surviving years of public cryptanalysis with a comfortable security margin. That's why you use AES and ChaCha20, and never a cipher that hasn't had that ordeal.

    20.5Tor and onion routing: hiding who talks to whom#

    HTTPS hides what you say, but everyone on the path still sees who you're talking to (Chapter 12). A VPN hides that from your café and internet provider, but the VPN provider sees everything instead. Onion routing spreads the trust so that no single computer knows both who you are and where you're going.

    The idea was developed at the US Naval Research Laboratory in the 1990s. Tor ("The Onion Router"), run by thousands of volunteer relays, made it available to everyone in the early 2000s.

    How the pieces from earlier chapters fit:

    • Your client builds a circuit one relay at a time, doing a separate key exchange (based on X25519, Chapter 10) with each relay, so each layer has its own key.
    • Each relay's layer uses symmetric encryption (Chapter 5); replies come back the same way, gaining a layer at each hop, and your client removes all three.
    • Onion services (addresses ending in .onion) never leave the Tor network at all. A modern onion address is an encoding of the service's Ed25519 public key (Chapter 11), so the address itself proves you reached the right server: no certificate authority needed.

    Its limits:

    • The exit relay sees your traffic to the website. If the site isn't HTTPS, the exit can read and change it. Use HTTPS inside Tor.
    • Traffic correlation. An adversary who can watch both your connection and the website's (say, a big network operator or a government) can match the timing and size of packets. Tor makes this hard, not impossible.
    • You can still identify yourself. Logging into your usual accounts or using a browser with a unique fingerprint undoes the anonymity. That's why the Tor Browser makes every user look alike.

    🧪 Try it yourself: with Tor running locally (brew install tor on macOS, or install Tor Browser), check that your traffic really goes through it:

    Terminal
    torsocks curl https://check.torproject.org/api/ip
# {"IsTor":true,"IP":"185.220.101.4"}      ← the exit relay's address, not yours
    ✏️ sketching an interactive demo…
    ⚖️ Pros & Cons

    Hiding who you talk to

    👍 Situational
    HTTPS alone

    Encrypts content

    • Everywhere, automatic
    • Hides pages, forms, cookies
    • IP addresses and the site’s name still visible
    Best for: Everyday browsing
    👍 Situational
    VPN

    One encrypted tunnel to one provider

    • Hides traffic from café Wi-Fi and your ISP
    • Fast
    • The VPN provider sees everything instead
    • One point of trust and of failure
    Best for: Untrusted networks, company access
    ✅ Use it
    Tor

    Three relays, three layers of encryption

    • No single relay knows both ends
    • Onion services need no CA
    • Slower
    • Exit relay sees non-HTTPS traffic
    • Global traffic correlation is possible
    Best for: Anonymity and censorship circumvention
    ❌ Avoid
    Plain web proxy

    Forwards requests for you

    • Changes your apparent IP
    • Often unencrypted
    • The proxy sees and can change everything
    Best for: Not for privacy

    20.6Logging in everywhere: Kerberos, SAML, OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect#

    Chapter 16 covered how you prove who you are (passwords, codes, passkeys). Big organizations and the web also need single sign-on: log in once, then use many services without each one seeing your password. Four standards dominate.

    Kerberos: tickets at the office. Created at MIT in the 1980s and the default in Windows Active Directory since 2000.

    It's all symmetric cryptography plus a trusted third party (Trent from Chapter 1). Tickets expire, usually after about 10 hours.

    📜 True story: Kerberoasting (2014). Any logged-in user can request a service ticket for any service, and that ticket is encrypted with a key derived from the service account's password. Security researcher Tim Medin showed that attackers can take those tickets offline and brute-force them. Service accounts with weak passwords fall in minutes, which is why they need long random passwords (Chapter 8). And if attackers ever steal the KDC's own master key (the krbtgt account), they can forge "golden tickets" for anyone.

    SAML: signed XML for enterprise web apps. SAML 2.0 (2005) lets a company's identity provider (such as Okta, Microsoft Entra ID or Google Workspace) log you into hundreds of cloud apps. After you log in, the identity provider sends your browser a signed XML document (an "assertion") saying who you are; the app checks the signature (Chapter 11) against the identity provider's certificate.

    ⚠️ Watch out: XML signatures are notoriously tricky. "Signature wrapping" attacks smuggle an unsigned, forged assertion next to a genuinely signed one and trick sloppy parsers into reading the forgery. And whoever steals the identity provider's signing key can sign in as anyone, anywhere: the "Golden SAML" technique seen in the 2020 SolarWinds intrusions.

    OAuth 2.0: "let this app access my account". When a calendar app asks "Allow access to your Google Calendar?", that's OAuth 2.0 (2012). It's about authorization (granting access), not login. The app never sees your password; it receives a limited, revocable access token.

    OpenID Connect (OIDC): login built on OAuth. OIDC (2014) adds identity on top: alongside the access token, the identity provider issues an ID token, a signed JWT (Chapter 16) that says "this is alice@example.com." That's what "Sign in with Google/Apple/Microsoft" uses.

    The recommended flow is the authorization code flow with PKCE ("pixy"):

    If a malicious app or a leaky log steals the authorization code in step 2, it's useless without the verifier, which never traveled through the browser. That's a one-way hash (Chapter 6) doing security work in plain sight.

    🧪 Try it yourself (Python): make a PKCE pair, and check the official test value from RFC 7636.

    Python
    import base64, hashlib, secrets

def challenge_for(verifier: str) -> str:
    digest = hashlib.sha256(verifier.encode()).digest()
    return base64.urlsafe_b64encode(digest).rstrip(b"=").decode()

verifier = base64.urlsafe_b64encode(secrets.token_bytes(32)).rstrip(b"=").decode()
print("code_verifier :", verifier)               # kept secret by the app
print("code_challenge:", challenge_for(verifier))  # sent in the login redirect

print(challenge_for("dBjftJeZ4CVP-mB92K27uhbUJU1p1r_wW1gFWFOEjXk"))
# E9Melhoa2OwvFrEMTJguCHaoeK1t8URWbuGJSstw-cM   ← matches RFC 7636, Appendix B
    Standard Year Format Used for Typical home
    Kerberos 1980s Binary tickets, symmetric keys Logging into office networks and file servers Windows Active Directory
    SAML 2.0 2005 Signed XML assertions Enterprise single sign-on to web apps Okta, Entra ID, Google Workspace
    OAuth 2.0 2012 Access tokens Letting an app access an account (authorization) APIs everywhere
    OpenID Connect 2014 Signed JWT ID tokens "Sign in with…" (authentication) Consumer and modern enterprise apps

    ⚠️ Watch out: OAuth on its own does not tell an app who you are. Apps that treated "I received an access token" as "the user logged in" have been tricked with tokens issued to other apps. Use OpenID Connect for login, validate the ID token's signature, issuer and audience, and use PKCE. The older "implicit flow," which put tokens directly in browser URLs, is now discouraged by the OAuth security best practices (RFC 9700, 2025).

    ⚖️ Pros & Cons

    Single sign-on standards

    👍 Situational
    Kerberos

    Tickets from a Key Distribution Center

    • Password never crosses the network
    • Mature, built into Windows
    • Kerberoasting and golden tickets
    • Built for one organization’s network
    Best for: Office networks (Active Directory)
    👍 Situational
    SAML 2.0

    Signed XML assertions

    • Supported by almost every enterprise app
    • XML signature wrapping bugs
    • Stolen signing key = Golden SAML
    Best for: Existing enterprise SSO
    ✅ Use it
    OAuth 2.0

    Delegated access tokens

    • Apps never see your password
    • Limited, revocable access
    • Not a login protocol on its own
    • Many options to misconfigure
    Best for: Letting an app use an API on your behalf
    ✅ Use it
    OpenID Connect

    Signed ID token on top of OAuth

    • Standard “Sign in with…”
    • JWT ID tokens anyone can verify
    • Must validate signature, issuer, audience, expiry
    Best for: Modern web and mobile login (with PKCE)
    ❌ Avoid
    Implicit flow

    Tokens returned in the browser URL

    • Simple for old single-page apps
    • Tokens leak via history, logs and referrers
    • Discouraged by RFC 9700
    Best for: Replace with code flow + PKCE

    20.7Paying with a card: EMV chips, contactless and tokens#

    A card's magnetic stripe stores fixed data: card number, expiry, a check value. Copy it once (a hidden "skimmer" on an ATM) and you can make a perfect clone. The EMV chip standard (named after Europay, Mastercard and Visa) fixes this with cryptography.

    What the chip does on every payment:

    1. The terminal sends the transaction details plus a fresh random number, the unpredictable number.
    2. The chip combines them with its transaction counter (which goes up by one every time) and computes a MAC (Chapter 7) using a secret key that never leaves the chip. This MAC is called the ARQC (Authorization Request Cryptogram).
    3. The bank, which can derive the same card key from its master key inside an HSM (Chapter 19), recomputes and checks it.

    A skimmer can copy the card number, but not the key. A recorded cryptogram is useless later, because the amount, unpredictable number and counter will differ: replay protection, exactly as in Chapter 18. Chips can also prove they're genuine offline using RSA signatures and a small certificate chain from the payment network (Chapter 13).

    Contactless cards and phones use the same cryptograms over radio. Apple Pay and Google Pay add tokenization: the phone never stores your real card number. It holds a substitute "device account number," and a secure chip in the phone generates a one-time cryptogram for each payment. If a merchant is hacked, the stolen token is useless elsewhere. Your PIN gets its own protection: payment terminals typically encrypt it with a fresh key for every transaction, derived with a scheme called DUKPT (Derived Unique Key Per Transaction), so a compromised terminal can't decrypt earlier PINs.

    📜 True story: when "unpredictable" wasn't. In 2012, researchers at the University of Cambridge found that some ATMs generated the "unpredictable number" with a weak counter-like generator. Anyone who could predict it could get a cloned card to precompute valid cryptograms in advance (a "pre-play" attack) and use them later. It's Chapter 4's lesson again: the whole design collapses when randomness fails. The same group had shown in 2010 that a man-in-the-middle device could make some terminals accept any PIN.

    ✏️ sketching an interactive demo…
    ⚖️ Pros & Cons

    Ways to pay

    ❌ Avoid
    Magnetic stripe

    Static data

    • Works everywhere, even old terminals
    • One swipe through a skimmer = a perfect clone
    Best for: Fallback only
    ✅ Use it
    Chip (EMV)

    Fresh cryptogram per payment

    • Key never leaves the chip
    • Replays fail (counter + unpredictable number)
    • Implementation flaws have let terminals accept wrong PINs
    • Weak terminal randomness enabled pre-play attacks
    Best for: In-person payments
    ✅ Use it
    Contactless

    Same cryptograms over radio

    • Fast; same chip security
    • Relay attacks possible in theory
    • Spending limits without PIN
    Best for: Small everyday payments
    ✅ Use it
    Phone wallet (tokenized)

    Device token + secure element

    • Real card number never stored or shared
    • Biometric check per payment
    • Depends on phone security and the platform
    Best for: Best everyday option
    ⚠️ Legacy
    Typing card number online

    Card-not-present

    • Universal
    • Static number can be stolen and reused
    • Needs extra checks (3-D Secure)
    Best for: With 3-D Secure or tokenized checkout
    ✔ section read

    20.8Trusting the device: secure boot, measured boot and attestation#

    All the cryptography in this guide assumes the software running it is honest. Malware that loads before the operating system (a "bootkit") could see every key. Three techniques build trust from the moment you press the power button.

    Secure boot: check each signature before you run it. A tiny piece of code in read-only memory, the root of trust, verifies the digital signature (Chapter 11) of the firmware; the firmware verifies the bootloader; the bootloader verifies the operating system kernel. If any signature is wrong, startup stops. UEFI Secure Boot on PCs keeps a list of allowed signing keys (db) and a revocation list of banned ones (dbx). Apple devices and Android phones ("Verified Boot") use the same chain-of-trust idea.

    Measured boot: write down a fingerprint of each step. Instead of only allowing or blocking, the TPM chip (Chapter 19) keeps a running hash of everything that loaded, in registers called PCRs:

    Like a blockchain (Chapter 16), each value depends on everything before it. Change one byte of the bootloader and every later value changes. The TPM can also refuse to release a secret (for example, the disk-encryption key behind BitLocker) unless the PCRs match the known-good values.

    🧪 Try it yourself (Python): simulate three PCR "extend" steps.

    Python
    import hashlib

pcr = bytes(32)                                        # PCRs start at all zeros
for stage in [b"firmware v1.2", b"bootloader v2.06", b"kernel 6.8"]:
    measurement = hashlib.sha256(stage).digest()
    pcr = hashlib.sha256(pcr + measurement).digest()   # "extend"
    print(stage.decode().ljust(18), pcr.hex()[:16], "…")
# firmware v1.2      5d816df843726846 …
# bootloader v2.06   029a2705d0dcd16e …
# kernel 6.8         0eac0b47b054574c …

    On Linux you can look at the real thing: mokutil --sb-state shows whether Secure Boot is on, and sudo tpm2_pcrread sha256:0,7 (from tpm2-tools) prints your PCRs.

    Remote attestation: prove it to someone else. The TPM signs the current PCR values with a key that can't leave the chip (a "quote"). A server can then check, remotely, that a device booted genuine software before letting it onto a company network. The same idea lets cloud customers verify confidential-computing enclaves (Chapter 17) before sending them secrets.

    📜 True story: BlackLotus (2023). Security firm ESET found the first publicly known bootkit able to bypass UEFI Secure Boot on fully updated Windows 11. It exploited an old, legitimately signed but vulnerable Windows boot component that had been patched, but not yet added to the dbx revocation list, so the firmware still trusted it. Revocation is just as hard for boot code as for certificates (Chapter 13).

    ✏️ sketching an interactive demo…
    ⚖️ Pros & Cons

    Device trust

    ✅ Use it
    Secure boot

    Verify each stage’s signature

    • Blocks unsigned bootkits
    • Simple yes/no decision
    • Vulnerable signed code must be revoked (BlackLotus)
    • Can restrict installing your own OS
    Best for: Every PC and phone
    ✅ Use it
    Measured boot

    Hash every stage into TPM PCRs

    • Detects any change, even signed ones
    • Can seal disk keys to known-good state
    • Legitimate updates change the values
    • Needs someone to check the measurements
    Best for: BitLocker, Linux disk unlock
    👍 Situational
    Remote attestation

    Prove boot state to a server

    • Zero-trust device checks
    • Verify cloud enclaves before sending secrets
    • Privacy and platform lock-in concerns
    • Complex to deploy
    Best for: Company devices, confidential computing
    ✔ section read

    20.9Hiding that a message exists: steganography#

    Encryption hides what a message says, but everyone can see that a secret message exists. Steganography ("covered writing" in Greek) hides the message's existence.

    It's ancient: the Greek historian Herodotus tells of a message tattooed on a messenger's shaved head, delivered once the hair had grown back. Digital versions hide data in places nobody looks:

    • Least significant bits of an image. Changing the lowest bit of a pixel's color changes it by 1 out of 255, invisible to the eye. A 12-megapixel photo has room for megabytes of hidden data.
    • Unused space in files, the timing between network packets, or tiny spacing changes in text.

    🧪 Try it yourself (Python): hide a message in the lowest bits of "pixel" values.

    Python
    import os

def hide(pixels: bytearray, secret: bytes) -> bytearray:
    bits = [(byte >> i) & 1 for byte in secret for i in range(7, -1, -1)]
    out = bytearray(pixels)
    for i, bit in enumerate(bits):
        out[i] = (out[i] & 0xFE) | bit          # overwrite the least significant bit
    return out

def reveal(pixels: bytes, length: int) -> bytes:
    bits = [p & 1 for p in pixels[:length * 8]]
    return bytes(int("".join(map(str, bits[i:i+8])), 2) for i in range(0, len(bits), 8))

image = bytearray(os.urandom(1000))             # pretend these are pixel values
stego = hide(image, b"meet at 5")
print(max(abs(a - b) for a, b in zip(image, stego)))   # 1: no pixel changed by more than 1
print(reveal(stego, 9))                                  # b'meet at 5'

    Where it shows up for real:

    • Malware hides commands and code inside innocent-looking images to slip past filters.
    • Watermarking embeds an owner's or recipient's ID in images, audio and documents, so leaks can be traced.
    • Many color laser printers print a nearly invisible pattern of tiny yellow dots encoding the printer's serial number and a timestamp, as the EFF documented in 2005.

    ⚠️ Watch out: steganography is not a substitute for encryption. Steganalysis tools detect the statistical fingerprints that hiding leaves behind, and once the hiding place is found, the message is in plain sight. If you use it, encrypt first, then hide, so even a discovered message is unreadable.

    ✏️ sketching an interactive demo…
    ⚖️ Pros & Cons

    Hiding vs. encrypting

    👍 Situational
    Steganography

    Hide that a message exists

    • Doesn’t draw attention
    • Steganalysis detects statistical traces
    • Found = readable, unless also encrypted
    Best for: On top of encryption, never instead
    ✅ Use it
    Encryption

    Hide what a message says

    • Proven, standard, strong
    • Everyone can see a secret exists
    Best for: Always
    👍 Situational
    Watermarking

    Hidden owner or recipient ID

    • Traces leaks back to the source
    • Can sometimes be removed or forged
    • Privacy concerns (printer dots)
    Best for: Media and document leak tracing

    20.10The crypto wars: export rules, key escrow and backdoors#

    Strong encryption protects everyone equally, including people that governments want to monitor. That tension has produced decades of conflict, often called the crypto wars.

    Round 1: crypto as a weapon (1970s–2000). The US classified strong encryption as a munition, alongside missiles. Software sold abroad was limited to deliberately weak "export-grade" crypto, typically 40-bit keys: Netscape shipped a strong "US edition" and a weak "international edition" of its browser.

    • After Phil Zimmermann released PGP in 1991 (Chapter 2) and it spread abroad, he faced a three-year criminal investigation, dropped in 1996.
    • In 1995, PGP's source code was printed and exported as a book, because printed books were protected as speech while software wasn't.
    • In 1999, a US appeals court sided with Daniel J. Bernstein (the designer of ChaCha20 and Curve25519), treating source code as protected speech. In 2000, the rules were substantially relaxed.

    Today, mass-market and open-source encryption can generally be exported, though some paperwork and country restrictions remain (international coordination happens through the Wassenaar Arrangement). The old rules still did damage: the FREAK and Logjam attacks of 2015 (Chapter 18) exploited export-grade options that servers had forgotten to remove 15 years later.

    Round 2: key escrow and the Clipper chip (1993). The US government proposed the Clipper chip for phones: strong encryption, but with a copy of every device's key held in escrow by the government, released for authorized wiretaps. In 1994, researcher Matt Blaze showed the escrow mechanism could be bypassed, because the field that carried the escrowed key information was protected by only a 16-bit checksum that could be brute-forced. Industry and public opposition was fierce, and the plan was quietly abandoned by 1996.

    Round 3: "going dark" (2010s–today). As phones, disks and messaging apps adopted strong encryption by default (Chapter 16), law enforcement warned of evidence "going dark" and asked for exceptional access: a way to unlock encrypted data with a court order.

    • 2016: the FBI asked a court to order Apple to write software unlocking a terrorist's iPhone. Apple refused; the FBI eventually got in with help from an outside firm and dropped the case.
    • 2015: a group of leading cryptographers published Keys Under Doormats, arguing that any exceptional-access system adds complexity and a high-value target that attackers will seek.
    • 2015: Juniper Networks found unauthorized code in its firewall software. Investigators concluded that the constants of the Dual_EC random generator (Chapter 4) had been changed by unknown attackers: a suspected backdoor taken over by someone else.
    • Some laws now let governments order companies to assist with access (for example, the UK's Investigatory Powers Act). In 2025, Apple withdrew its Advanced Data Protection end-to-end encrypted backups for UK users after reportedly receiving such an order. Proposals in several countries to scan messages on users' devices before encryption ("client-side scanning") remain hotly debated.

    💡 Key idea: Mathematics can't tell a lawful investigator from a criminal or a hostile government. A key held "only for the good guys" is a key that can be stolen, leaked or abused, which is why most cryptographers oppose backdoors. The policy debate weighs that risk against real investigative needs, and it isn't over.

    ⚖️ Pros & Cons

    The policy debate: arguments on each side

    💡 Concept
    Exceptional access

    Key escrow / lawful-access mechanisms

    • Could help investigate serious crimes when data is otherwise unreadable
    • Courts could oversee each use
    • Creates a high-value key or mechanism to steal or abuse
    • History: Clipper flaw, hijacked Dual_EC at Juniper
    • Other governments will demand the same
    Best for: Hotly debated
    💡 Concept
    Strong encryption by default

    No one but the user holds the keys

    • Protects everyone: citizens, businesses, journalists, governments
    • No master key to leak
    • Can hinder investigations (“going dark”)
    • Lost keys can mean lost data
    Best for: The default in modern phones and messengers
